opus-5.5.text:
I think the key reason is that the two are fundamentally different kinds of constraints. Training speed is largely an engineering and compute problem. If you have more GPUs, better infrastructure, better parallelism, you can make training faster. That matters, of course, but in some sense it's a problem that money and engineering effort can keep pushing on.

Token efficiency is different. The amount of high-quality data in the world is limited. We've already consumed a large fraction of the good text on the internet, and the growth rate of new high-quality data is much slower than the growth rate of compute. So if you look a few years ahead, the real bottleneck isn't how fast you can run a training step. It's how much intelligence you can extract from each token you have. If your architecture or optimizer can learn the same thing with, say, half the tokens, that's effectively like doubling your data, and data is the thing you can't just buy more of.

That's why we've spent a lot of effort on things like optimizers and architectural improvements. When we worked on the Muon optimizer at scale, for example, the goal wasn't just faster wall-clock convergence. It was to get a better loss for the same number of tokens. Once you think of it this way, every improvement in token efficiency raises the ceiling of what the model can eventually reach, whereas pure speed improvements mostly just get you to the same ceiling sooner.

There's also a deeper point. I believe the essence of intelligence is something like compression, extracting more structure from less information. Humans learn from far fewer tokens than our models do. So improving token efficiency is, in a way, pushing models closer to what real intelligence should look like. It's not only a practical matter of data scarcity; it's also a more principled direction.

And then there's the agentic era. When models start generating their own data, interacting with environments and doing reinforcement learning, each trajectory is expensive to produce. So learning efficiently from every token becomes even more important. To me, token efficiency is one of the most important levers for continuing to scale intelligence when the easy scaling resources start running out.

r001.rationale: The response describes token efficiency as extracting more intelligence from each token and learning the same thing with fewer tokens, thereby making better use of a fixed amount of training data.

r002.rationale: It says pure speed improvements mostly reach the same ceiling sooner, while token efficiency improves the result for the same number of tokens.

fable-5.1.text:
Because data, not compute, is the real bottleneck now. The internet is finite. High-quality tokens are finite. Compute keeps getting cheaper, and clusters keep getting bigger, but you can't manufacture more internet. So if you look at the whole scaling curve, the thing that will run out first is not FLOPs, it's data.

When you think about it that way, the question changes. It's no longer "how fast can I train a model," it's "how much intelligence can I extract per token." That is the number that determines where the ceiling is. If two labs have the same data and one of them gets twice as much capability out of each token, the second lab's advantage compounds. Faster training only gets you to the same ceiling sooner.

There is also a deeper reason. Token efficiency is essentially a measure of how good your learning algorithm is. Humans are extraordinarily token-efficient. A child doesn't read trillions of words to learn language. So the gap between human learning and current pretraining is a signal that the method is still crude. Whenever I see a large gap like that, I think that's where the research opportunity is. Things like better optimizers, better architectures, better data mixtures, RL on top of pretraining, these are all really ways of raising token efficiency.

And practically, it fits a smaller team. Kimi can't out-GPU the biggest players. But if we can be smarter about every token we touch, that's a lever that doesn't depend on who has the largest cluster. So it's both the scientifically correct question and the strategically correct one for us.

r001.rationale: The response frames token efficiency as how much intelligence or capability a model gains from each token, including comparing capability on the same data.

r002.rationale: It says faster training reaches the same ceiling sooner, while greater capability comes from extracting more from the same data.

astra-6.text:
I think training speed is only one part of the equation. You can process more tokens per second, but if you need more tokens to reach the same level of capability, you haven’t necessarily made learning more efficient. Token efficiency asks: how much can the model learn from a given amount of data?

That matters because high-quality data and compute are both limited. If we can reach the same performance with fewer tokens, we reduce the total training cost. And with the same budget, we can potentially build a more capable model. So making training faster is valuable, but I also want to improve how effectively the model learns.

r001.rationale: Defines token efficiency as how much the model can learn from a given amount of data, and says fewer tokens can achieve the same performance.

r002.rationale: Says training speed is only one part of efficiency, but does not state that speed alone cannot raise the intelligence ceiling for a fixed training token budget.

sol-6.1.text:
Because making training faster and making better use of tokens are two different things. You can improve the infrastructure and process the same data in less time, which is valuable. But token efficiency asks: how much intelligence can the model gain from a given amount of data and computation?

If we can reach the same capability with fewer tokens, we reduce the resources needed to get there. Or, with the same budget, we can train a more capable model. So I see training speed as an important engineering goal, while token efficiency gets at the learning process itself: how do we make each token contribute more?

r001.rationale: It defines token efficiency as how much intelligence a model gains from a given amount of data and computation.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes processing the same data faster from learning more per token, but does not clearly state that faster training alone cannot raise the model’s intelligence ceiling under a fixed token budget.
